cards.front: Why is it better to make a method abstract than to give it a body that throws an error?
cards.back: The compiler catches the mistake; a runtime throw waits until the method is called
cards.extra: An error-throwing stub only fails when someone runs it, and only if the test suite happens to reach it. abstract fails at compile time, for every subclass.

cards.front: A subclass of an abstract class does not implement every abstract method. What happens?
cards.back: It stays abstract itself, and must say so
cards.extra: You may deliberately leave the job to a further subclass, but then the compiler requires the abstract keyword on this one too.

cards.front: Can a class be abstract without any abstract methods?
cards.back: Yes — it simply cannot be instantiated
cards.extra: The book uses it to prevent objects of a class whose only purpose is to be a common base. No unimplemented methods are required.

cards.front: When would you choose an abstract class over an interface?
cards.back: When subclasses must share state or partial implementation
cards.extra: An abstract class can hold fields and finished methods; an interface is a pure contract. That is why the book calls the abstract class the midway step.

cards.front: What does an interface contain, conceptually?
cards.back: Only the contract — method signatures with no implementation
cards.extra: A class that implements it promises those methods exist. Callers can then be written against the interface and work with every implementation.

cards.front: A class implements two interfaces with the same method signature. How many methods must it write?
cards.back: One — a single implementation satisfies both contracts
cards.extra: Signatures are identical, so one method fulfils two promises. This is why multiple interface inheritance avoids C++'s diamond problem: there is no state to duplicate.
